claims.text: A 46-year-old man had a cochlear implant placed in the right ear in 2013 because of profound binaural sensorineural hearing loss. Five years after the implant he presented with otorrhoea of 8 months duration in the implanted ear. The implant had been functioning normally, but otoscopic examination revealed an electrode array protruding through the external auditory canal.

claims.text: Endoscope-assisted revision surgery via the posterior external auditory canal covered the exposed electrode and repaired the broken posterior canal wall. A tragal cartilage-perichondrium graft was harvested, ear wax, pus and scabs were removed, the field was disinfected, the electrode array was confirmed well positioned within the cochlea, rotated and pushed back into the mastoid cavity, and the graft was inserted through the perforation before the meatus was packed.

the patient was treated by endoscope-assisted revision surgery via the posterior external auditory canal to cover the exposed electrode array with a cartilage/tragal perichondrium graft
The patient agreed to endoscopic revision surgery to cover the exposed electrode in the mastoid cavity and to repair the broken posterior wall of the external ear canal.
The entire procedure was performed under endoscopic guidance.
A composite tragal cartilage–perichondrium graft was harvested and submerged in normal saline.
Ear wax, pus and scabs were removed endoscopically
the external auditory canal, mastoid cavity and exposed electrode [Figure 1] were disinfected by washing three times with compound lysostaphin disinfectant
The soft tissue around the electrode was cleaned to release the electrode array and expose the mastoid cavity [Figure 2a].
Exploration via the facial recess confirmed that the electrode array was well positioned within the cochlea [Figure 2b].
The exposed electrode array was carefully rotated to reverse its spiral movement and then gently pushed back into the mastoid cavity.
The mucosa around the broken external ear canal wall was carefully scarified with a serrated circular knife to prepare a bed for the graft [Figure 2c].
To repair the external ear canal wall, the composite tragal cartilage–perichondrium graft was inserted through the perforation with the perichondrium facing the external auditory canal [Figure 2d].
The meatus was packed with gelfoam and an iodoform gauze strip.
